newsitem.title: CHINA: Three ASEAN ministers meet Cambodia's Sihanouk.
newsitem.headline: Three ASEAN ministers meet Cambodia's Sihanouk.

text.p: Three Southeast Asian foreign ministers arrived at the Beijing residence of Cambodia's King Sihanouk on Thursday for talks on the crisis in his homeland after a bloody coup earlier this month.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines arrived separately at Sihanouk's palatial residence in the former Legation Quarter of Beijing on Thursday morning.

The three ministers, mandated by the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to meet Sihanouk to try to promote a negotiated settlement in Cambodia, had said they would meet among themselves before beginning talks with Cambodia's king.
Officials of the Cambodian king's entourage refused to comment and diplomats at the three embassies refused to give details of what was expected from the talks.
Sihanouk, who reigns but does not rule in Cambodia, has requested secrecy around his talks, officials said. The king has been receiving medical treatment in Beijing.
The three foreign ministers were due to meet their Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen later in the day.
"We have come here to listen to the king," Thailand's Prachuab said on his arrival late on Wednesday.
"We will listen to Sihanouk's views and suggestions on how we can help to find solutions if all parties in the dispute are willing," Alatas said in Jakarta before leaving for Beijing.
"We don't have any recipe to solve the problem...so we will listen to his views," he said.
Alatas said the ASEAN ministers would convey the decision to postpone Cambodia's entry and listen to Sihanouk's views on the situation in Cambodia.
Sihanouk has been holding court at his Beijing residence, meeting two officials of Group of Seven (G7) nations, from Japan and France, this week to brief them on the crisis in Cambodia.

Sihanouk also sent a letter on Tuesday to acting head of state Chea Sim in Phnom Penh, calling for an end to murder and bloodshed in the conflict between Second Prime Minister Hun Sen and his son, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, who was deposed in Hun Sen's July 6 coup.
In Phnom Penh, a diplomatic source said as many as 40 Cambodians have been killed since the overthrow of Ranariddh but it was not clear if the killings were part of a planned purge.
The source, who declined to be identified, said there was evidence of torture among some of the victims, including four bodyguards of Ranariddh's top military commander, General Nhiek Bun Chhay.
The guards were found dead with their eyes gouged out.

Sihanouk said in his letter he was distressed by the reports of torture and killings and urged that those detained or arrested as enemies of the state be treated in line with the law and in accordance with provisions of relevant international treaties.
Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh, Sihanouk's son, on July 6 after a weekend of fighting in the capital. Ranariddh left Cambodia a day before the coup.

In what political analysts see as a bid to legitimise his takeover, Hun Sen has said he wants to preserve the coalition between his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) and Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC. He said he did not want the job of first prime minister and FUNCINPEC must choose a replacement for Ranariddh.
